1. Injury of the Teeth: Dental Caries and Periodontal Disease

Dental caries

  • Focal demineralization and decay of a tooth from acidic byproducts (e.g., lactic acid) made by normal oral bacteria, especially Streptococcus mutans, during carbohydrate fermentation (more sugar → more acid → more demineralization).
  • Progression: white spot on the surface → decay into enamel (a cavity) → dentin → pulp → risk of infection at the base of the tooth (abscess).
  • Prevention: good oral hygiene and fluoride (strengthens teeth against acid).
Dental caries (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)

Periodontal disease

Chronic inflammation of the supporting structures of the tooth.

StageWhat happens
1Bacteria and saliva build a biofilm: dental plaque; plaque mineralizes into tartar (calculus)
2Plaque/tartar irritates the gingiva (gums): gingivitis
3With more plaque and gum recession, inflammation spreads to the rest of the periodontium: periodontitis
  • Complications: damage to the periodontal ligaments → loose teeth and tooth loss; periodontal infection → systemic spread (infective endocarditis, distant abscess such as in the brain).
Periodontal disease (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)

2. Soft Tissue Inflammation: Aphthous Ulcers, Reactive Lesions, Lichen Planus, Pemphigus Vulgaris

Aphthous ulcers (canker sores)

  • Common, recurrent inflammatory lesions of the oral mucosa; cause not fully known but multifactorial.
  • Risk factors: family history; immune disorders (celiac disease, inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), Behcet disease).
  • Gross: shallow ulcer with a thin fibrinopurulent exudate and a red (erythematous) halo.
  • Resolve on their own in about 7–10 days; immunocompromised patients: longer, may need treatment.
Aphthous ulcer (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)

Reactive lesions

Non-infectious inflammation of the mucosa or gingiva producing fibrous nodules.

LesionFeatures
Irritation fibromaRepetitive trauma (e.g., biting the cheek, along the bite line); smooth pink exophytic nodule
Pyogenic granulomaRed-purple, highly vascular, may ulcerate; children/young adults, most associated with pregnancy ("pregnancy tumor"); can regress or become a peripheral ossifying fibroma
Peripheral ossifying fibromaLooks similar but calcified; most common in young women; can develop from a pyogenic granuloma
Peripheral giant cell granulomaLooks like pyogenic granuloma grossly; histology: abundant multinucleated giant cells in a vascular stroma
Reactive lesions (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)

Lichen planus

  • Chronic inflammatory condition of skin, nails, hair and mucous membranes (not only the mouth). Oral disease: age 50–60, slight female predominance. Associated with hepatitis C.
  • Skin: papules. Oral: Wickham striae (white lines on the inside of the cheek).
Lichen planus (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)

Pemphigus vulgaris

  • Systemic autoimmune disease with oral and skin vesicles and bullae.
  • IgG autoantibodies against desmoglein (DSG) 1 and 3, which hold epithelial cells together → loss of cell-cell adhesion (acantholysis).
  • Presentation depends on the DSG3:DSG1 ratio: the oral cavity expresses more DSG3, so it shows erosions; the skin shows blisters.
Pemphigus vulgaris (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)

3. Oral Infections: Herpes and Candidiasis

Oral herpes

  • Herpes simplex virus 1 (HSV-1) (HSV-2 is mostly genital).
  • Children (2–4 y/o): gingivostomatitis. Adults: pharyngitis (sore throat).
  • Virus stays latent in neurosensory ganglia. A stressor (trauma, allergies, pregnancy) causes reactivation = recurrent herpetic stomatitis: small vesicles at the same site; example: herpes labialis (cold sore). Resolves in 7–10 days; immunosuppressed patients may need antiviral therapy.
Oral herpes (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)
DiagnosisFindings
Immunohistochemistry (IHC) for HSV-1 on a biopsyMultinucleated keratinocytes
Tzanck test (scrape the base of a vesicle)Multinucleated keratinocytes + intranuclear (eosinophilic) inclusion bodies

Complications: vesicle ulceration; corneal ulceration (can lead to blindness) with repeated infection.

Oral herpes diagnosis (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)

Oral candidiasis

  • Candida albicans is part of the normal oral flora in about half of people; overgrowth occurs in immunocompromised patients: HIV/AIDS, newborns, prolonged antibiotics, chemotherapy-induced neutropenia, diabetes.
FormFeatures
Pseudomembranous (thrush)Most common; white membrane that scrapes off; any mucosal surface
ErythematousFlat red patches on the tongue or hard palate
HyperplasticWhite plaque (buccal mucosa, lips, sides of tongue) that does not scrape off
Angular cheilitisDry, cracked corners of the mouth; not specific to candidiasis (other drying conditions, medications)
Oral candidiasis (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)

4. Premalignant Lesions: Leukoplakia, Hairy Leukoplakia, Erythroplakia

LeukoplakiaHairy leukoplakiaErythroplakia
LesionWhite plaque that cannot be scraped off and is not explained by another cause (candidiasis, lichen planus)White, "hairy" patches on the lateral tongueRed, often velvety or eroded; bleeds when scraped
CauseTobacco and alcohol (causal); other chronic irritationEpstein-Barr virus (EBV) in immunosuppressed patients (80% HIV; also transplant or cancer therapy)Tobacco and alcohol
Frequency / risk~3% of the population; 5–25% are premalignant (dysplasia)Benign, not premalignantHigh risk of dysplasia (90%) and malignant transformation
HistologyHyperkeratosis; with or without dysplasia (hyperchromatic, crowded, disorganized cells)Hyperkeratosis + parakeratosis (retained nuclei); balloon cells(High-grade dysplasia)
  • Leukoplakia and erythroplakia can coexist: nonhomogeneous lesion / erythroleukoplakia. Biopsy is needed to confirm dysplasia and decide next steps.
  • Hairy leukoplakia is often used to help identify HIV.

5. Squamous Cell Carcinoma (SCC)

  • Malignancy of squamous epithelium; 95% of head and neck cancers are SCC (HNSCC).
  • Causes: tobacco and alcohol (synergistic when combined), betel quid (Southeast Asia), human papillomavirus (HPV): 90% of oropharyngeal SCC but <5% of oral cavity SCC.

Non-HPV-associated SCC

  • Arises in a background of premalignancy (leukoplakia, erythroplakia, erythroleukoplakia); mutagens give a high tumor mutational burden; TP53 and RB mutations.
  • Gross: ulcerated, exophytic, indurated. Microscopic: keratinizing, keratin pearls, malignant epithelial islands invading (e.g., into muscle) with immune infiltrates.
Non-HPV-associated SCC (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)
Non-HPV-associated SCC histology (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)

HPV-associated SCC

  • No premalignant lesion; lower mutational burden; driven by the HPV oncoproteins E6 and E7; p16 (CDKN2A) overexpression.
  • Mechanism: normally RB holds back E2F; cyclin D–CDK4 phosphorylates RB, freeing E2F and driving G1→S. p16 inhibits cyclin D–CDK4 (a brake that rises as the cycle progresses). E7 binds and sequesters RB regardless of phosphorylation → E2F is constitutively active → unchecked proliferation, and p16 rises (uselessly). So p16 IHC is a diagnostic marker; HPV mRNA in situ hybridization also confirms.
  • Primary tumors are small; microscopic: nonkeratinizing, basaloid nests, no keratin pearls; lymph node metastasis is common (a palpable node is often the first sign).
HPV-associated SCC (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)
HPV-associated SCC histology (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)

Comparison

Non-HPV-associatedHPV-associated
CauseTobacco, alcohol, betel quidHPV infection (sexually transmitted)
Tumor siteOral cavity: tongue, floor of mouth, lower lip, soft palate, gingivaOropharynx: tonsils, tongue base, soft palate, pharynx
MorphologyGross: ulcerated, within a precancerous lesion, exophytic, indurated. Micro: keratinizing, epithelial islands, immune infiltratesGross: small, not within a precancerous lesion. Micro: nonkeratinizing, basaloid nests, p16 overexpression
PrognosisPoor due to field cancerization, distal metastasisGood (or at least better) due to isolated tumor formation; local cervical lymph node metastasis but limited distal metastasis

Clinical

  • Field cancerization: chronic mutagen exposure of the whole mucosal surface causes multiple independent primary tumors; removing one does not remove the others.
  • Metastasis: cervical lymph nodes (local); distal: mediastinal nodes, lungs, liver, bone (more in non-HPV disease).
  • Treatment: surgery + adjuvant radiation; immunotherapy is emerging. PET-CT shows the tumor well (glucose uptake).

7. Salivary Glands: Xerostomia and Sialadenitis

Xerostomia (dry mouth)

  • Reduced saliva production. Causes: Sjögren syndrome (autoimmune; lymphocytic infiltration of salivary and lacrimal glands; dry eyes and dry mouth; diagnosed by anti-SSA, anti-SSB, rheumatoid factor), radiation therapy to the head and neck, and, most commonly, medication side effects (analgesics, sedatives, antidepressants).
  • Complications: dental caries, candidiasis, difficulty swallowing and speaking.

Sialadenitis (inflammation of the salivary glands)

CauseFeatures
Trauma: mucocelePseudocystic lesion from mucin leaking out of a ruptured excretory duct; most common on the lower lip (swelling with a blue hue); floor of mouth = ranula. Histology: mucin-filled cavity with granulation tissue lining and an intact gland nearby. Treatment: complete excision
Obstruction: sialolithiasisSialolith (stone-like formation: impacted food debris, local edema, or unknown cause) → impaired flow → chronic unilateral inflammation; can progress to Staphylococcus aureus infection
Infection: mumpsParamyxovirus; fever, pain, swelling of the salivary glands; usually self-limited but can cause systemic inflammation (ovaries, testes, pancreas, brain: meningitis/encephalitis); vaccine-preventable
Sialadenitis: mucocele (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)
Sialolithiasis (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)
Mumps (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)

8. Salivary Gland Neoplasia

GlandShare of tumorsMalignant
Parotid65–80%Mostly benign
Submandibular~10%~40%
Sublingual (and minor glands)<10%70–90%
Rule of thumbRisk of malignancy is inversely related to gland size: tumors are most common in the big glands, but the smaller glands are most likely to be malignant.

Pleomorphic adenoma (PA)

  • Benign mixed tumor of epithelial, myoepithelial and mesenchymal (stromal) cells. Most common salivary tumor, usually parotid. "Pleomorphic" means many cell types, not malignancy.
  • Pathogenesis: radiation exposure; chromosomal rearrangements causing PLAG1 overexpression (pleomorphic adenoma gene 1; detected by break-apart FISH), or HMGA2 rearrangement/mutation when PLAG1 is not overexpressed.
  • Gross: painless, slow-growing, mobile, often <6 cm; solid, well-circumscribed, tan-yellow cut surface.
  • Micro: usually encapsulated; triphasic (ducts lined by epithelial cells, myoepithelial cells, stroma that may be myxoid, chondroid or chondromyxoid). Some have pseudopods into the surrounding gland → recurrence after resection.
  • Clinical: diagnosed by biopsy and imaging (well-defined homogeneous mass); treated by surgical excision; incomplete removal → recurrence (multiple nodules). Rare transformation to carcinoma ex pleomorphic adenoma: ~2% if present <5 years, up to 10% if >15 years; high mortality.
Pleomorphic adenoma: PLAG1 FISH (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)
Pleomorphic adenoma histology (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)
Pleomorphic adenoma clinical (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)

Warthin tumor

  • Benign; oncocytic epithelial cells lining papillary and cystic structures within a lymphoid stroma (papillary cystadenoma lymphomatosum). Second most common salivary tumor, almost always parotid.
  • Usually unifocal; ~10% multifocal or bilateral. Strong association with smoking, especially bilateral tumors.
  • Micro: papillary projections, cystic spaces (may contain mucin), dense lymphoid stroma with germinal centers, bilayered epithelium (columnar on the cystic side, cuboidal on the lymphoid side); oncocytes have abundant mitochondria (hazy cytoplasm).
Warthin tumor histology (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)

Mucoepidermoid carcinoma (MEC)

  • Malignant; mucinous, epidermoid (squamous) and intermediate cells. Most common malignancy of the salivary glands (~15% of salivary tumors); ~65% in the parotid, also minor glands.
  • CRTC1::MAML2 fusion gene in about 50% (thought to alter Notch signaling).
  • Grade tracks morphology: low-grade = more cystic, lots of mucinous cells; high-grade = more solid (epidermoid and intermediate cells), mitotic figures, necrosis.
GradeBehavior
Low~15% locally invade or recur; distal metastasis rare; ~90% 5-year survival
IntermediateOutcomes similar to low-grade; morphology similar to high-grade
HighLocal invasion common; ~30% recurrence; ~30% distal metastasis; ~50% 5-year survival
Mucoepidermoid carcinoma histology (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)
Mucoepidermoid carcinoma clinical (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)

Adenoid cystic carcinoma (ACC)

  • Malignant; epithelial and myoepithelial differentiation. 50% arise in minor salivary glands (not exclusive to salivary glands: also sinuses, larynx, breast; can also arise in parotid/submandibular). Grossly poorly circumscribed.
  • Driven by MYB::NF1B or MYBL1::NF1B fusion genes (MYB oncogene overexpression); the fusion is often diagnostic.
PatternFeatures
CribriformEpithelial cells interrupted by hyalinized globules (mostly myoepithelial cells)
TubularDuct-like structures lined by epithelial cells and surrounded by myoepithelium
SolidNests or sheets of mostly epithelial cells; most aggressive, higher grade, NOTCH1 mutation, bone and liver metastasis
  • Perineural (and intraneural) invasion is characteristic. Slow growth with late distal recurrence (e.g., lung; ~50%); survival ~65% at 5 years, 30% at 10, 15% at 15 years.
Adenoid cystic carcinoma patterns (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)
Adenoid cystic carcinoma clinical (lecture slide) (click to enlarge)

Comparison

PAWarthinMECACC
BehaviorBenignBenignMalignantMalignant
LocationParotidParotidParotid or minor glandsMinor glands, also major glands
Molecular driverPLAG1 or HMGA2N/ACRTC1::MAML2MYB::NF1B or MYBL1::NF1B
MicroscopicEpithelial, myoepithelial and stromal cells (mixed); pseudopodsBilayered oncocytes, papillary structures, cystic spaces with lymphoid stromaMucous, epidermoid and intermediate cells; solid vs cysticCribriform, tubular, solid patterns

9. Study Guide Key: Guiding Questions and Feature Matching

Guiding questions (from the study guide)

Why might chronic periodontal disease lead to tooth loss?Chronic inflammation destroys the periodontal ligament and the supporting tissues; the tooth loosens and is eventually lost.
Why is oral disease so common in immunocompromised patients, and which lesions are typical?The mouth is an entry point for opportunistic organisms and the immune system normally controls them. Typical lesions: aphthous ulcers, oral herpes, oral candidiasis (white, scrapes off), hairy leukoplakia (lateral tongue, does not scrape off).
Canker sores vs cold sores: similarities and differences?Similar: painful, ulcerate, recurrent, resolve in about 7–10 days (unless immunocompromised). Different: canker sores are not viral and occur on non-keratinized mucosa (e.g., inside the lip); cold sores are HSV-1 and occur on the lips; cold sores can cause corneal ulceration.
Why does oral herpes recur at the same site?The virus becomes latent in neurosensory ganglia; stressors reactivate it, and it returns to the same site.
Presentations of oral candidiasis?Pseudomembranous (thrush): white, scrapes off. Erythematous: flat red patches. Hyperplastic: white plaque that does not scrape off. Angular cheilitis: dry corners of the mouth.
Leukoplakia vs hairy leukoplakia?Same: white lesions that do not scrape off. Different: hairy leukoplakia is caused by EBV in immunosuppressed hosts (80% HIV), occurs on the lateral tongue, and is benign; leukoplakia is associated with tobacco/alcohol and is premalignant in 5–25%.
Leukoplakia vs erythroplakia?Same: do not scrape off; tobacco and alcohol; malignant potential. Different: white vs red; erythroplakia has a much higher risk of dysplasia and malignant transformation (about 90% dysplasia).
SCC that arises in erythroplakia: what do you expect?Most likely non-HPV-associated SCC: severe dysplasia and atypia, malignant squamous cells in nests or cords with keratinization / keratin pearls.
HPV-associated vs non-HPV-associated oncogenesis?HPV: E6/E7 oncoproteins; E7 inhibits RB → constitutive E2F → cell cycle progression and p16 overexpression. Non-HPV: mutagens (tobacco, alcohol) → accumulated mutations (TP53, RB) → no p16 overexpression.
Odontogenic lesions: name and describe three.Dentigerous cyst (crown of an unerupted tooth); radicular/periapical cyst (inflammatory, at the apex of a damaged tooth); odontoma (benign hamartoma of tooth material); ameloblastoma (cystic epithelial tumor, benign or malignant).
What is Sjögren syndrome and how does it cause xerostomia?Autoimmune disease with lymphocytic destruction of salivary and lacrimal glands; inflammation and tissue damage reduce saliva production.
Three causes of sialadenitis?Trauma (mucocele), obstruction (sialolith; can progress to S. aureus infection), infection (mumps paramyxovirus).
Cell types of PA and MEC, and what raises concern for malignancy?PA: epithelial, myoepithelial, stromal; long-standing tumors (15+ years) have the highest risk of carcinoma ex pleomorphic adenoma. MEC: epidermoid, intermediate, mucinous; the more solid the tumor, the higher the grade.
What is perineural invasion and why does it matter in ACC?Tumor cells spreading along or around nerves; characteristic of ACC; promotes local spread and recurrence.
